articles.title: Footage of Tibet floods isn't being shown in China - and we know little about victims there
articles.summary: Some of the most dramatic footage from the deadly flash flooding is hidden from public view in China.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: China censors videos showing deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border By Laura Bicker China correspondent ,  Reporting from Beijing 
- Published 28 August 2026 Updated 29 August 2026 04:54 BST 
The dramatic footage was almost impossible to miss. A torrent of water tearing through Gyirong Port, one of the main border crossings between Nepal and Tibet, sweeping away all in its path as hundreds of people fled for their lives. 
The scenes, captured by CCTV cameras, quickly spread on social media and onto screens around the world. 
Except here, in China. 
Only a single still-frame shot has been broadcast so far by the country's state-run flagship news bulletin. 
It has also been difficult to find the video on China's heavily censored internet. It is just as hard to even find posts describing the flash flooding that has claimed hundreds of lives, with just as many still unaccounted for since Wednesday. 
- 
Follow live updates 
Beijing has launched a massive rescue operation involving hundreds of emergency workers, which is continuing, and President Xi Jinping chaired an emergency meeting with officials to co-ordinate efforts. 
But when you compare the country's internet content to what much of the world has been seeing online these past few days, China's firewall becomes more visible than ever. 
Tibet, which Beijing annexed in the 1950s, had long resisted rule by the Chinese Communist Party. 
China has quashed protests over the years, sometimes violently, and has been accused of grave rights violations in the Buddhist region. It has labelled the exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, a separatist. 
That history means the very name Tibet draws China's censors. Beijing's sensitivities are especially apparent at times likes this. 
Figure caption, 
Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet border 
There have been daily updates on the missing and the dead, and Beijing has also been posting updates on the rescue operations, as well as the dangers posed by a barrier lake that has been at risk of overflowing. 
On Saturday, new footage from Chinese state media showed rescue teams wandering in a wasteland of mud and rock while calling out to anyone trapped. 
But there is little detail beyond that. There are no accounts from survivors in Tibet, and almost no user-generated footage showing the deadly moments or their aftermath. 
We are yet to hear from anxious families of those missing. Trying to contact people there is near-impossible during regular times. 
As a journalist who has covered North Korea, it has often been easier for me to contact interviewees in Pyongyang than it is in the Tibetan capital, Lhasa. 
Image source, Reuters 
On Thursday night, as global headlines led on the devastation in a Himalayan valley, China's state broadcaster opened its main bulletin with the launch of Xi's new book, a selection of his "most important and fundamental works". 
Foreign journalists cannot travel to Tibet without government permission. We have just a few hours to get as much information as we can on huge stories like this before videos are scrubbed and voices stifled. 
Instead, we have to rely on state media, which has so far focused on incredibly dramatic rescue efforts. 
Specialist search teams scaling mountains and cliff faces, or crossing raging rivers to try to get to the worst-affected areas. We don't yet know what happened afterwards, or who they were able to save. 
This is not to say that Beijing is unconcerned. Rather, they are very concerned. 
China's Premier Li Qiang was quickly despatched to the region, where he was seen inspecting debris removal - a rare visit by the country's second-most important leader so soon after a major disaster. 
The reason for what the world might see as a muted response is to preserve the one thing Xi covets for his country: stability. 
The Communist Party will fear that such a disaster could fuel discontent, either with the response or the lack of foresight to prevent it. 
It may also fear the impact of a tragedy like this and its potential to be a rallying factor, especially in a community where faith has long played a central role. 
Although the region has not seen protests in a long time, Tibetan groups abroad have expressed concern over increasing Chinese control, such as new education laws that they say aim to weaken the role of monasteries and the Buddhist faith. 
Image source, Gongga Laisong/China News Service/VCG via Getty Images 
Just hours after the disaster struck, the Communist Party machine tried to rally its grassroots to stem any signs of discontent of its handling of the landslide. 
A notice came from the local party office urging members to step up and help in disaster relief efforts in their area and provide emotional guidance or psychological support to affected residents. 
The key line instructs them to "make every effort to maintain social order and ensure stability and public confidence in the disaster areas". Those who perform well would be rewarded - and those who do badly "would be held accountable". 
It is a warning that will not be taken lightly. Tibetans in the region can be detained or arrested for speaking to journalists or posting anything online that is seen as contrary to the government narrative, according to rights activists. 
That is making it difficult for Tibetans outside the region to find out what has happened to their relatives. 
The International Campaign for Tibet, while praising the work of first responders in the area, said Beijing had been removing videos and other first-hand information from social media. It called on Chinese authorities to "disclose complete and verifiable information about the damage and casualties". 
To try to understand what life is like for Tibetans, the BBC travelled to a town that sits on the edge of the Himalayan plateau last year - just outside what China calls the Tibetan Autonomous region. 
There, we spoke to monks at the Kirti monastery in Aba, or Ngaba in Tibetan, which was once at the heart of its resistance to Beijing. "We Tibetans are denied basic human rights," one monk told us. 
They said they lived under constant surveillance and claimed the Chinese government oppressed and persecuted Tibetans. The conversations were brief because we could not be seen speaking to anyone for long. 
Beijing denies it is violating Tibetans' rights, and points to the heavy investments it has made in the region to boost tourism and integrate it with the rest of the country. 
Nevertheless, people in China will not know very much about what is happening in Tibet right now.

articles.title: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
articles.summary: Hundreds have died and thousands are missing after Wednesday's flooding and landslides on the border of Nepal and Tibet.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet border By Olivia Ireland ,  Henry Moore   and   Amy Walker 
- Published 26 August 2026 Updated 29 August 2026 12:47 BST 
Devastating landslides and flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have caused widespread damage and left hundreds dead and thousands more missing. 
More than 600 people have been killed and at least 2,400 people remain unaccounted for, according to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. 
At least seven people have died in Tibet, with another 554 reported missing by Chinese state media. 
On Wednesday, flood water tore through the border region, sweeping away homes and roads, local officials have said. 
Rescue workers say they now face a critical moment to reach remaining survivors as fears mount of further flooding in the disaster's aftermath. 
Here is what we know so far. 
- 
Follow live updates 
- 
Tracing the deadly path of the Nepal-Tibet flash flood 
- Published 2 days ago 
- 
She was about to cross into Tibet for a long-awaited pilgrimage - then her messages stopped 
- Published 1 day ago 
What caused the landslide? 
Initial reports of an earthquake on the Nepal-Tibet border led many to believe that a tremor had caused a landslide, which in turn caused the devastating floods early on Wednesday. 
However, the US Geological Survey (USGS) later confirmed that the disaster was caused by a "glacial collapse" - when a glacier or part of a glacier disintegrates. 
The impact of the collapsed glacier hitting the bottom of a valley was so powerful that it registered a magnitude of 5.2, according to the agency, causing "subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream". 
Powerful flood water and debris travelled some 62 miles (100km) downstream from the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi Rivers, the USGS said, sweeping through towns popular with mountaineering tourists and pilgrims in northern Nepal. 
Footage showed a wall of mud and rock sweeping away buildings, roads and vehicles as people fled in the Nuwakot region. 
In one video, a towering wall of water and mud was seen rushing down a gorge along the Trishuli River and enveloping the Rasuwagadhi Border checkpoint, a multi-storey building on the Nepalese side. 
Gyirong Port, over the border, was also hit. A number of deaths were reported in Tibetan villages. 
Scientists are trying to piece together the exact order of events as rescue efforts continue. Mike Searle, professor of Earth sciences at Oxford University, said the glacier could have collapsed "hours or days" before the flooding hit Nepal and Tibet. 
"I think the sheer wave of debris suggests there was a landslide first, the water built up, [which] dammed the river, and then it burst in one huge great flood," he told the BBC. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: What caused the Nepal-Tibet flash floods? 
The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIDMOD) has warned secondary flooding could occur in the coming days as a result of debris that washed into the river systems. 
The ICIDMOD said it was assessing whether the Trishuli River had been temporarily blocked in narrow sections. If this is the case, it is at risk of forming a landslide dam and a second flood. 
Separately, China has warned there was a "high risk" a lake that formed after the landslide may burst its banks, causing fresh flooding downstream. As of Friday, an estimated 2.5 million cubic metres of water had accumulated, according to broadcaster CCTV. 
State media reported that rescue operations were briefly suspended on Friday after the lake, which has formed at the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers, overflowed - before water levels dropped slightly. Heavy rain is forecast over the next few days. 
But experts have told the BBC that it was possible that the lake could drain naturally over time. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: The lake prompting fears of second flood in Nepal 
How many people are dead and missing? 
The number of people killed or missing is still becoming clear. 
At least 616 people had died as of Saturday, according to Nepali police, while the country's disaster agency has said at least 2,426 people are still missing. 
The government has released a list of more than 517 foreign nationals who have been out of contact since the floods hit. 
Meanwhile, seven people have died in Tibet and 554 are missing, China's state broadcaster CCTV has reported. These figures have not been independently verified. 
Tibet, which China annexed in the 1950s, is one of the most strictly controlled regions in the country. It is virtually impossible for foreign media to gain entry there and trying to contact local residents is just as hard. 
It is unclear whether any of the missing in the Nepali and Chinese figures have been counted twice. 
Brigadier General Rajaram Basnet, a spokesman for Nepal's army, told the BBC that rain and unpredictable weather in the area were making rescue operations increasingly challenging. 
Which countries are the missing tourists from? 
Figure caption, 
Aerial footage shows flash flood on Nepal-Tibet border 
Tourists from all over the world come to Nepal for its mountains and sacred sites. Reports of those missing include the following: 
- 
India - at least 320 Indian nationals are missing, the foreign ministry in Delhi says 
- 
China - The Chinese foreign ministry says nearly 100 Chinese nationals are missing in Nepal 
- 
US - 90 Americans are still missing, the US state department says 
- 
Ukraine - 62 Ukrainian nationals are missing, Nepalese police say 
- 
Malaysia - 51 Malaysians travelling with Fishtail Tours and Travels are missing in the floods, officials say 
- 
Australia - 41 Australians are unaccounted for, according to the country's assistant immigration minister 
- 
UK - Nepal's police say 33 British nationals are missing 
- 
Canada - 30 Canadians are missing, says the country's foreign ministry 
Smaller numbers of travellers from countries including South Korea, South Africa, Portugal, the Netherlands and New Zealand have also been reported missing. 
How are governments responding? 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Police officers were pictured carrying a survivor from the flash floods in Nepal's Nuwakot district 
Nepal's priority is to locate the missing and provide urgent relief, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said on Saturday, with more than 4,450 people rescued so far. 
He said authorities were co-ordinating with families to identify those missing, and diplomats were facilitating communications with the relatives of missing foreign nationals. 
He said the risk of possible secondary flooding was being monitored, with officials on "high alert". 
Additional personnel were deployed on Friday in the hopes of speeding up recovery efforts, the office of Prime Minister Balendra Shah said. 
Chinese President Xi Jinping chaired an emergency meeting of officials to co-ordinate rescue efforts the same day, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua. 
Kamal Kishore, special representative of the UN secretary general for disaster risk reduction, urged countries to support response efforts. 
The US previously promised $500,000 (£367,982) in aid for communities affected by the floods, while the UK said it had offered £5m. 
Meanwhile, the Indian Air Force said that military cargo planes carrying nearly 50 tonnes of supplies had been sent to Nepal. 
Might climate change have played a role? 
Climate change is known to be driving faster glacier melt in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region. 
Geologist Daniel Shugar – one of the first experts to suggest Wednesday's flash flooding could have been caused by glacial activity – said glacial thinning caused by global warming could increase the risk of landslides. 
But it is still too early to definitively link the event to climate change, Shugar, who is based at the University of Calgary in Canada, told the BBC. 
Simon Cook, a geoscientist at the University of Dundee, said that climate change "could have an impact". 
He said his team believed they had identified where the collapse had occurred. He told the BBC that the lower part of a glacier in Nepal near the Langtang Lirung peak - approximately 15km west of the site of the floods - had collapsed. 
Cook estimated that the glacier collapsed in a north-westerly direction and then travelled westwards downstream. 
He told the BBC that "permafrost is partially holding some mountainsides together, this permafrost is warming and thawing and degrading so you are going to get more landslides".

articles.title: Chinese artist jailed over satirical Mao sculptures, say rights groups
articles.summary: The case against Gao Zhen, who was prosecuted under a law banning "slander of heroes", has been seen as an assault on artistic freedom.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Xiao Ke Image caption, 
Gao Zhen was arrested in 2024 By Kelly Ng 
- Published 26 August 2026 
A Chinese artist known for his satirical sculptures of Mao Zedong has been handed a maximum three-year jail term for "slandering China's heroes", according to rights groups. 
A court in Hebei province had ruled on Tuesday that Gao Zhen's work "infringes upon the hero's reputation and harms public interest". 
Among the 70-year-old's most famous pieces, produced with his brother Gao Qiang, is a sculpture comprising a squad of Mao-like figures holding Jesus Christ at gunpoint. 
Gao has been in detention for the past two years, and the UN and many rights groups have called for him to be released. Amnesty International has called his sentencing an "assault" on artistic freedom. 
Gao had moved to the US in 2022 but was arrested at his studio on the outskirts of Beijing during a visit in August 2024. 
Authorities seized his artworks and barred his wife and seven-year-old son from leaving China. 
China watchers have said that Gao Zhen's arrest shows how the Chinese Communist Party is becoming increasingly extreme in both grasp and reach – including by policing its citizens transnationally and retroactively. 
He was charged under a law that came into force in March 2018, which bans the defamation of historical figures associated with the party. 
The Gao brothers' Execution of Christ sculpture was exhibited in 2009, as were two other sculptures cited in the case. 
They are Mao's Guilt, a life-sized replica of the leader kneeling in a pose of solemn contrition; and Miss Mao which depicts him with large breasts and a long, Pinocchio-style nose. 
Gao's case was heard in a one-day, closed-door trial earlier this year, which received limited coverage in China. 
He plans to appeal the conviction, Amnesty International said on Tuesday. 
If the verdict is upheld, Gao would be due to complete his sentence in August 2027 as it would take into account the two years that he has already spent in detention. 
Image source, Supplied Image caption, 
The Gao brothers (pictured) rose to prominence in China's art scene during the 1990s and 2000s, earning a global reputation for works that skewered the politics of their homeland 
"No artist should face criminal punishment for creating work that challenges official narratives or encourages critical reflection on history," Amnesty International's China Director Sarah Brooks said on Tuesday. 
"This trial demonstrates how broadly worded and politically motivated laws are used – and worse, in this case, used retroactively – to silence artists, activists and other individuals who dare to express views that differ from those of the Chinese government," she said. 
"The case against [Gao Zhen] raises particular concerns with regard to the retroactive application of criminal law, the use of criminal sanctions to punish artistic expression, and the impact on his family," the UN's Human Rights Office told AFP news agency. 
Earlier this year, his brother Gao Qiang told the BBC that the trial's "message is clear". 
"Even if a work was made 15 years ago, it can still be turned into a crime if today's political climate changes," he said.

articles.title: Why Tesla has been caught up in a massive car recall in China
articles.summary: The country's biggest ever car recall affects more than four million vehicles made by Tesla, XPeng, Xiaomi and other firms.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Hidden door handles were popularised by Tesla By Osmond Chia Business reporter 
- Published 26 August 2026 
Hidden car door handles - the sleek designs often found on electric vehicles (EVs) - have come under the spotlight over the past week. 
That's after China announced its biggest ever recall of cars, with more than four million vehicles - mostly Teslas - affected . 
The recall comes ahead of new regulations in China , requiring cars to have a mechanical release both on the inside and outside of their doors. 
Popularised by Elon Musk's electric vehicle giant, this type of handle has become commonplace around the world. 
But several incidents have raised concerns that this design may make doors difficult to open in an emergency. 
'A real safety concern' 
Hidden door handles are widely used in modern cars in China, with around 60% of the top 100 best-selling new energy vehicles, including EVs and hybrids, having them. 
The minimalist design gives vehicles a "sleek look and reduces wind drag" but can be confusing to use, car industry analyst Stephen Dyer from consultancy AlixPartners told the BBC. 
"Even I often find it difficult to locate the switch to open the door from the inside of an unfamiliar vehicle," said Dyer, who is based in Shanghai. 
But beyond their usability, the handles have been blamed for endangering the lives of drivers and passengers. 
Electronically powered door handles became an industry trend, but raised "real safety concerns" when doors failed to open promptly, delaying rescue efforts after accidents, said Nanyang Technological University associate professor Lyu Chen. 
"A door handle may seem simple, but it becomes safety-critical in the seconds after a crash," Chen said. 
Chinese carmaker Xiaomi faced intense scrutiny following two fatal crashes in 2025 involving its SU7 model, when suspected electrical failures allegedly trapped occupants. 
One of the incidents took place on a highway in Tongling city, eastern China, killing three people, according to regional news coverage cited by state-controlled media Global Times. 
Relatives of the victims said the passengers were stuck in the car as the vehicle's doors could not be unlocked after the collision, the outlet said. 
Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, 
The SU7 was Xiaomi's first electric vehicle 
At the time, Xiaomi's representatives said the SU7 had mechanical emergency release handles that function even without power, which are located at the bottom of each door. 
The company added at the time that it was investigating the matter and cooperating with the police. 
The latest models of the SU7 come with new door handles that can be opened without power. 
Xiaomi has not responded to BBC requests for comment. 
Tesla has also faced lawsuits in the US over its door handle designs. 
The company has been sued by the only survivor of a crash in 2024 involving a Cybertruck - Tesla's electric pickup - that killed three college students in California. 
Survivor Jordan Miller alleged that the Cybertruck's design trapped passengers in the burning vehicle and blocked their rescue. 
The car did not have door handles and the electronic buttons meant to open the doors failed to work, according to his lawyers from The Veen Firm. 
"When you design a vehicle with no mechanical way to open the doors from the outside, you are betting the electronics will work in every scenario, including a high-speed crash followed by a fire," said one of the lawyers in a statement. 
In court filings, Tesla denied any wrongdoing and said the Cybertruck is compliant with US federal safety standards, the Guardian reported. 
There have been other cases in the US of passengers, including children, allegedly being trapped in Tesla cars after the doors suddenly stopped working. 
The BBC has contacted Tesla for comment. 
What is being done about hidden handles? 
In February, China said it would ban hidden door handles, making it the first country to do so. 
The new rules, which take effect on 1 January 2027, mean new car designs without physical release mechanisms on the inside and outside of their doors cannot be sold. 
The cars' interior must also carry signs to show how to open the door. 
The measures in China come ahead of the US and European Union, which typically lead regulations around road safety and emissions, Dyer noted. 
One reason is likely to be the sheer number of EVs in China, he added. 
On 21 August, China's State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) announced that Tesla and some major Chinese car makers - including Xiaomi, XPeng and Geely - would recall more than four million vehicles. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
China will ban hidden door handles on cars sold in the country from next year 
The manufacturers were ordered to add warning labels inside vehicle doors to show passengers how to open them. Some cars will also get a software update that will lower their windows in the event of a crash. 
Tesla, which started selling the Model S sedan with hidden door handles in China in 2014, is recalling nearly three million cars, according to the SAMR. 
The agency said the recalled cars have door handles that are "difficult to identify" because they are a similar colour to the vehicle's interior trim. 
In the event of an electrical failure, the handles' design may also prevent passengers from quickly opening the doors to escape or "hinder rescue efforts" by bystanders, the SAMR added. 
Xiaomi, XPeng and Geely will also recall a total of more than 750,000 vehicles. 
'Weak remedy' 
Some engineers say the measures may not go far enough to resolve safety concerns. 
Engineering instructor Lim Hong Wee said the measures do not address the need for a mechanical way to open the doors. 
Access to a car during an emergency should not depend on software, said Lim from the National University of Singapore. 
The measures mainly address the issue of people being able to get out of a vehicle, but do not provide a reliable way for rescuers to get in, said Gokul Krithivasan from risk management consultancy SecureSafe. 
Warning labels are also a "weak remedy", he added. "When panicked, people fall back on their instinctive responses, and don't read small print in a dark and possibly smoke-filled cabin." 
For now, it is unclear whether there will be similar recalls outside China. 
The BBC understands that carmakers have not yet notified authorities of any plans for a similar recall in the US.

The US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration told the BBC that it is reviewing whether it will require emergency door-exit systems in vehicles. 
In Europe, regulators have flagged the potential hazards related to hidden handles and drafted new standards to ensure they still work even if a car's power is cut off. 
Engineering lecturer Lyu Chen said that while concealed door handles are still common in EV designs, manufacturers and regulators are paying increasing attention to how they design their doors. 
Since cars are built to sell globally, it is likely that the safety requirements in China will be adopted elsewhere, he added. 
"The common principle is clear: emergency entry and exit should remain possible even after a loss of electrical power."

articles.title: Satellite images reveal scale of flood devastation in Nepal villages
articles.summary: Before-and-after images show villages, bridges and a key Nepal-Tibet border crossing washed away by devastating floodwaters.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Tracing the deadly path of the Nepal-Tibet flash flood By Paul Brown and Adam Durbin BBC Verify 
- Published 28 August 2026 
New satellite imagery has revealed the scale of the devastation along Nepal's Trishuli River caused by Wednesday's deadly flash flood, triggered by a glacier collapse. 
Before-and-after images show how sections of the valley, where a torrent of floodwater and debris surged through, destroyed villages, bridges and hydroelectric power stations. 
Hundreds of people have been killed and thousands more are missing, Nepalese officials say. 
Among the worst-hit locations reviewed by BBC Verify was a key Nepal-Tibet border crossing, which was engulfed by a rush of floodwater and captured on camera. 
The satellite imagery from US-based intelligence firm Vantor, shows the site has been almost entirely washed away. Shocking CCTV footage showed the moment as the deluge of water swept over buildings as people tried to escape. 
Damage and mud can be seen more than 2.5km (1.5 miles) upstream, reaching 100m (330 ft) above the area it first hit. 
A few miles further south is the village of Timure, which has now largely disappeared. 
The walls of the valley at this point are steep, reaching up to 50m above the water line. The image shows most of the houses perched on this slope are now gone or covered in mud. 
A further 10km (eight miles) downstream, where the Trishuli River winds through Syapru Besi, satellite imagery now shows the village covered by mud, rock and other debris. Houses and other structures have disappeared, including bridges and a hydroelectric power station. 
One of the larger villages to be struck by the full force of the flood was Trishuli, where some of the earliest verified footage of the disaster emerged from. 
A satellite image of the town and surrounding agricultural land, which is about 45km (28 miles) downstream from the border, show an entire neighbourhood has been essentially washed away. 
Verified videos of the town show a bridge collapsing as the river surges forward. At the very same moment from ground level, footage filmed from inside a bus shows people crying out in distress and trying to flee as they see the water rushing down the river. 
Other dramatic videos show people sheltering inside a house, peering over the edge of a balcony as they watch a torrent of floodwater wash away almost everything around them, knocking large metal debris and a vehicle toward the building. 
Somehow the house remains intact and survivors can be seen in a second verified video standing surrounded by mud once the floodwater had receded. 
Imagery from satellite provider Planet Labs released today has also provided a clearer view of the disaster's origins at the collapsed glacier, the moment of which has been captured on a verified drone video. 
The satellite image shows an enormous chunk of the glacier has fallen away, carving an enormous path of rock and debris where water rushed through the valley. 
At the base of the landslide, trees and other vegetation have been stripped at a height of more than 300m above the riverbed. 
This destructive path continues westwards along with the swelled river, before heading southwards. 
Satellite images also show the formation of a barrier lake at the base of the landslide's path, which Chinese authorities have warned poses a major risk of further flooding and has hampered rescue efforts. 
Dr Argha Banerjee, a glaciologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, told BBC Verify that it was not possible determine from the images how stable the barrier was or how likely the lake was to drain suddenly. 
But he said there was no significant increase in its surface area between Wednesday and Thursday, despite water continuing to flow into the lake. 
Dr Banerjee said there was a visible drainage channel, which suggests some water was already escaping downstream, adding that the its volume was "not alarmingly large" and appeared to have stabilised. 
The extent of the damage on the Tibetan side of the border remains unclear. It is a strictly controlled region which China annexed in the 1950s, where foreign media access is heavily restricted. BBC Verify has so far been unable find verifiable footage from the area. 
The satellite imagery - which only provides an initial glimpse into the damage of the flood - has been published by Vantor as part of its Open Data Program to help aid authorities establish where best to focus their efforts to locate the missing, rescue survivors and recover the dead. 
Additional reporting Shruti Menon, Merlyn Thomas and Alex Murray. Graphics by Mesut Ersoz and Mike Hill.

articles.title: 97-year-old woman rescued after Nepali floods looked like 'a warrior'
articles.summary: A 97-year-old woman, Guna Maya Bohara, survived the flash floods and was rescued using an excavator.
articles.full_text:
97-year-old woman rescued after Nepali floods looked like 'a warrior'
97-year-old woman rescued after Nepali floods looked like 'a warrior' 
Close 
A 97-year-old woman pulled from flood debris in Nepal is recovering in hospital, according to her doctors. 
Guna Maya Bohara's great-nephew, Dipak Bohara, has told BBC Nepali she looked like "a warrior" who had returned victorious from battle. 
The operation to pull Bohara out of the rubble of her care home took four hours. 
Bohara travelled from Kathmandu to help rescue his great-aunt. 
Hundreds of people have been confirmed dead after Wednesday's flash floods, which scientists believe were triggered by a glacier collapsing in the Himalayan border region with Tibet.

articles.title: The heartbreak of reporting from a camp housing Nepal flood survivors
articles.summary: A BBC Nepali reporter witnesses helicopters coming and going in one of the most flood-devastated areas.
articles.full_text:
Image caption, 
One woman rescued by the Nepali Army says her husband, father, and mother are still missing By Shreejana Shrestha BBC Nepali ,  Reporting from Nuwakot, Nepal 
- Published 28 August 2026 
I enter the camp to an absolutely heartbreaking scene. 
Hundreds of people are queuing outside, desperately trying to see if they can find their loved ones. 
This army camp in Nuwakot, one of the main districts in central Nepal affected by devastating flash floods and massive landslides, has been turned into a search-and-rescue centre. 
Inside, a woman cradling an infant in her arms is crying hysterically. Her entire family, including her father, husband and mother, are all missing. She is traumatised, and in so much pain. 
There are other people who have sustained injuries, and some who say they had miraculously survived. 
One driver who was working in Rasuwa tells us he'd been thrown into the water when the floods hit. He still doesn't know how he managed to survive. Yet while thankful to be alive, he is also devastated - he's also lost more than 20 of his friends. 
When I try speaking to him he is unable to focus, and not in a proper state of mind. There are tears in his eyes. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
More than 400 people have died after flash floods hit the Nepal-Tibet border 
At one point while filming, a woman - perhaps in her 60s or 70s - is taken out of a helicopter and brought to the centre to be treated. 
She suddenly collapses. I later learn she has died. It is tremendously difficult to describe what I witnessed. 
Every hour at the camp there are dozens of helicopters coming and going, and many people are receiving treatment. 
Whenever these helicopters come, people look at them with a ray of hope their loved ones will be inside. 
Even as the helicopters land, blowing gusts of wind and mud down on everyone, people still don't look away - trying to catch a glimpse of who's on board. 
Image caption, 
At least 12 helicopters were mobilised by Nepal's government to continue search and rescue operations, according to officials 
After we leave the camp we try to get access to the internet so we can share what we've seen, but internet connectivity is extremely poor, so we drive about three hours back to our office in Kathmandu. 
Disasters are something I have covered several times in Nepal, but this is one of the most harrowing I have ever seen. 
But as a journalist you do your job: you receive information and report what you see.

articles.title: 'High risk' of lake breaching and causing second flood, warns China
articles.summary: Authorities say a lake formed after a recent landslide near the Nepal-Tibet border may breach in the coming days.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: The lake prompting fears of second flood in Nepal By Tessa Wong Asia digital reporter 
- Published 28 August 2026 
China has warned there is a "high risk" a lake that formed after the recent landslide near the Nepal-Tibet border may breach its banks, causing a second flood downstream. 
The warning comes after Wednesday's deadly flash flood in the same area, which scientists say was triggered by the collapse of a mountain glacier into a river . 
As of Friday, an estimated 2.5 million cubic metres of water had accumulated, according to broadcaster CCTV. Officials said that three million cubic metres of water was expected to flow into the lake between Thursday and the weekend, posing a "high risk of breach". 
But experts have told the BBC that it was possible that the lake could drain out naturally over time. 
China's Ministry of Water resources said that the barrier lake - a body of water formed when debris dams up a river - had formed at the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers. 
It is near the Langtang Lirung peak where the collapsed glacier is believed to have originated, and several kilometres upstream from Gyirong Port, the major land crossing linking Nepal and China which was hit by Wednesday's massive flood. 
The barrier lake had started to overflow on Thursday. Then on Friday morning, a Chinese military drone captured footage of an avalanche on a snow-capped mountain which deposited an estimated 50,000 cubic metres of ice debris into the barrier lake. 
Authorities issued warnings and orders to prepare for emergency evacuations. Rescue work was suspended as most of the Chinese emergency services stopped at a village about 7km (4 miles) from Gyirong Port. 
This was because the barrier lake at that time was "overflowing non-stop", which could lead to fresh floods or debris flows, according to a CCTV report. 
But by Friday afternoon, state media reported that the "risk from the upstream barrier lake had come under control" and that rescue operations had resumed. 
Authorities have since sent engineering teams to monitor the lake's water levels and the atmospheric conditions, and drones have been flown in to drop off equipment and supplies. 
Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist with the University of Graz who has researched lake bursts in Nepal, told the BBC there was still a possibility that the lake could breach its banks. 
"Not all the material on the mountain could have come down, it is still unstable, so there's a chance that something will drop," he said, adding that if the material dropped into the lake or even further upstream, "then we have a problem". 
Chinese state media have also reported there will be heavy rainfall and storms in the region in the coming days, raising concerns that this may cause the lake to swell. 
If the lake breaches its banks, there will not likely be a massive deluge of water as seen on Wednesday as the lake formed recently and was not very deep, said Steiner. 
However, the water discharged could further undercut the valley's slopes and cause more erosion - which could in turn cause more landslides. 
"Authorities need to be very careful for the rescue and prepared for any secondary wave and post-disaster landslides as the valley walls have been scoured and much more vulnerable," said Mohd Farooq Azam, a glacio-hydrologist with scientific institution the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development. 
Steiner said it was unlikely that the Chinese could stop the lake from overflowing. 
He pointed out that, while it was technically possible to artificially drain the lake using excavators, there were no proper roads that would allow them to transport heavy machinery to the lake's location.

But both experts said it was possible that the problem could eventually resolve itself. 
Azam pointed to recent flash floods in India's Chamoli and Dharali, where artificial lakes "drained slowly without much impact downstream". 
Similarly, "the only thing [China] can do is hope that the water will slowly drain out naturally" out of the barrier lake in Tibet, said Steiner. 
"And it will slowly drain – the melting season will be over by October so things are going to get calmer. There's going to be less water, and then by winter [what's left] will be all frozen." 
Separately, Nepali authorities have warned of the risk of blockages causing further floods along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers. 
They have warned people to stay away from the rivers until further notice. 
Scientists have said that the flood on Wednesday was likely to have been caused by part of a glacier near Langtang Lirung collapsing into the river below, which in turn caused a massive surge downstream carrying water and debris. 
Several hundred people have died in Nepal and with hundreds more still missing after the flash flood. On the Tibet side of the border alone, more than 550 are missing - nearly half of whom are foreigners.

articles.title: Why India wants Bangladesh's Tarique Rahman in Delhi
articles.summary: India is keen to reset ties with Bangladesh, but old tensions and new regional alliances complicate its efforts.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
India has been making concerted efforts to reset ties with Bangladesh's new government led by Tarique Rahman By Anbarasan Ethirajan Global Affairs Correspondent 
- Published 28 August 2026 
It is not often that an official email offers a glimpse into relations between two neighbouring countries. 
But a message from the Indian president's office earlier this month did just that, quickly catching the attention of diplomats and journalists. 
It said a weekend Change of Guard ceremony at the presidential palace had been cancelled because rehearsals were being held for the ceremonial welcome of Bangladesh's Prime Minister Tarique Rahman. 
There was just one problem: no visit had been officially announced. 
Within hours, the email was withdrawn , external . But it added to weeks of speculation over a possible visit by Rahman - and highlighted India's efforts to bring Bangladesh's new leader to Delhi. 
Rahman is yet to accept. "No decision has yet been made on the visit," AAM Saleh, the Bangladeshi prime minister's press secretary, told the BBC. 
India is keen to host the leader of its eastern neighbour for talks - and the timing matters. This would be Rahman's first visit since taking office after his Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) won a landslide victory in parliamentary elections in February. 
The vote marked a new political era in Bangladesh after the country's long-time leader Sheikh Hasina was ousted in a mass uprising in August 2024, in which hundreds of people were killed. She fled to India, where she has remained since. 
Relations between the two countries deteriorated sharply under the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus, which took over after Hasina's removal. 
Now, Delhi is hoping Rahman's government offers a chance to reset a crucial relationship - but Hasina's presence on Indian soil is making that harder. 
Bangladesh has asked India to extradite Hasina, who was sentenced to death in absentia by a special tribunal for ordering lethal force to be used against protesters during the uprising. She denies the charges. 
"We called for the creation of a propitious environment and are awaiting response from the Indian side regarding expediting extradition of Sheikh Hasina," Saleh said. 
India says the request is being considered. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Sheikh Hasina was ousted in a mass uprising in 2024 
Despite the issue, Delhi has made repeated overtures to the new government. A formal invitation was extended to Rahman soon after he took office, and India's High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi has held discussions with Bangladeshi officials, including the prime minister, in recent weeks. 
When Rahman visits, Trivedi has said , external , he will be "accorded the highest honour" and given a "memorable welcome". 
Such public enthusiasm is unusual for India, which does not often make such a strong show of wanting to host the leader of a neighbouring country. 
"I would imagine that there is a degree of frustration [in Delhi] because except for actually handing over Hasina, they have gone pretty far in terms of reaching out to Dhaka," Shyam Saran, a former Indian foreign secretary, told the BBC. 
Saran points to India's efforts to meet some of Bangladesh's immediate needs, including supplying electricity and fuel and issuing medical visas. Several bilateral mechanisms aimed at facilitating trade have also been revived, he said. 
Of course, there is a lot at stake for both countries. 
India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545-mile) border, as well as close cultural and linguistic ties. Bilateral trade was worth more than $12bn last year, overwhelmingly in India's favour. 
Bangladesh is also important to India's efforts to improve access to its north-eastern states. 
During Hasina's 15 years in power, the two governments expanded road, rail and port links, improving India's access to its north-east. They also worked closely on security, with Hasina's government cracking down on insurgent groups that India said had been operating from Bangladeshi territory. 
But India's close relationship with the former prime minister became increasingly controversial in Bangladesh, where critics accused Delhi of overlooking concerns about democracy and human rights. 
And her continued presence in India has kept those tensions alive. They resurfaced on 5 August, when Hasina addressed journalists virtually at an event organised by the Foreign Correspondents' Club of South Asia in Delhi. She vowed to return to Bangladesh in December and accused Rahman's BNP government of suppressing her supporters. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Sheikh Hasina, seen here with Narendra Modi, has been living in exile in India 
Bangladesh said it was "outraged" that she had been allowed to speak publicly on Indian soil. 
India's foreign ministry said it had "no role" in the event and did not "endorse anything said at the forum, especially with regard to the duly constituted government of Bangladesh". 
The timing was particularly sensitive. Lailufar Yasmin, a professor at Dhaka University, says there had been reports that Rahman was seriously considering a visit to India before Hasina's appearance. 
"It actually created a huge backlash in Bangladesh," she told the BBC. "Questions were raised whether Indian authorities were sincere about a reset in bilateral relationship." 
For Rahman, travelling to Delhi while Hasina remains there could therefore carry a political cost at home. 
But India's eagerness to repair ties is about more than Hasina. Since her removal, Bangladesh has also begun rebuilding relations with India's arch-rival Pakistan. 
Dhaka and Islamabad have exchanged high-level military visits and spoken publicly about expanding defence co-operation - developments being watched closely in Delhi. 
In the 2000s, India accused Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence agency of helping train insurgents from India's north-east in Bangladesh and assisting their movement across the border. Authorities in Pakistan and Bangladesh denied the allegations at the time. 
The recently announced Mecca pact - a defence agreement signed this month by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, three powerful Islamic countries - has also sparked interest from several nations, including Bangladesh. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545-mile) border 
The specifics of the agreement and the obligations on each party are not clear, but it is modelled on NATO's collective defence principle: that an attack on one member would be seen as an attack on all. 
"If there is a security arrangement among Islamic nations in the Middle East, it is not unusual for us to consider participating," Bangladesh's junior foreign minister Humayun Kabir told journalists this week. 
"It is being viewed positively." 
Saudi Arabia has also invited Rahman for a bilateral visit. It is not clear whether Bangladesh has been formally asked to join the defence agreement. 
Prof Yasmin says Dhaka should proceed carefully. "Bangladesh should be a bit cautious about entering into any defence pact," she says. 
"It's not just about antagonising India; Bangladesh needs to wait for a while to see which way it's going and whether it will align with our interests." 
For India, these developments are a reminder that its relationship with Bangladesh is changing, and that Delhi can no longer assume the exceptionally close relationship it enjoyed under Hasina. 
Rahman's government, meanwhile, has reasons to demonstrate that its foreign policy is not overly dependent on its giant neighbour. 
Prof Yasmin says Rahman should visit Delhi before the UN General Assembly meeting in New York in mid-September. 
"Neighbours have to live together," she says. 
There may soon be another opportunity. India is due to host a BRICS summit in mid-September and Bangladesh has been invited as a special guest. 
After weeks of invitations, diplomatic overtures - and one prematurely revealing email - Delhi will be hoping Rahman finally comes.
